{"id": "2:106/q23", "question": "Is خير comparative or a noun meaning good?", "turns_on": "Whether من expresses comparison or origin, and whether مثلها can coordinate.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q23/p1", "position": "Comparative: more beneficial than the earlier verse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Samīn favor this; coordination with 'or its like' is natural."}, {"id": "2:106/q23/p2", "position": "A good or benefit from the verse, with من marking origin.", "reasons": "Some compare 2:105 or 27:89, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn find coordination of 'its like' strained."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q24", "question": "What does the opening question do rhetorically?", "turns_on": "Confirmation, admonition, rebuke, or a genuine request for knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q24/p1", "position": "It confirms what the addressee knows about God's power.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites Arabic rhetorical usage; al-Baghawī calls it interrogative in form and affirmation in force. Abū Ḥayyān rejects making it need an omitted alternative. Al-Ālūsī says replacing a pronoun with Allah's proper name evokes awe and gathers the divine attributes."}, {"id": "2:106/q24/p2", "position": "It admonishes or rebukes denial of abrogation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī rejects the simple affirmation analysis; al-Zarkashī prefers rebuke directed to a denier, while another explanation treats it as commanding recognition."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q25", "question": "Who is addressed by 'do you not know'?", "turns_on": "Prophet alone, his community through him, any listener, or deniers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q25/p1", "position": "Muhammad is addressed, with his companions or community intended.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 2:104, 2:107, and 2:108 and Arabic singular-to-plural shifts; al-Kumayt and Jamīl's poems illustrate indirect address. Bursawī adds the Prophet's special knowledge."}, {"id": "2:106/q25/p2", "position": "Any accountable listener or especially the deniers of abrogation.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī and al-Ālūsī transmit these possibilities; the scope of God's power may be general or specifically support Muhammad against enemies."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q26", "question": "What does qadīr and 'everything' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the scope is absolutely general or understood to exclude impossibilities and God's attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q26/p1", "position": "God has power to change rules and provide whatever benefit He promises.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes ability from measuring; al-Jishumī calls qadīr intensive, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya says impossibilities and eternal attributes are not 'things' within the scope. The claim also supports divine sovereignty. Abū Ḥayyān says repetition of Allah marks independent clauses; the final denial of protector or helper and mention of power match the promised change. Elmalılı says divine unity reserves legislative repeal to God and grounds the Prophet's knowledge of omnipotence."}, {"id": "2:106/q26/p2", "position": "The conclusion specifically reassures the Prophet of help against enemies.", "reasons": "Some link God's unrestricted power to support and vengeance as well as legal replacement."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q27", "question": "Does abrogation imply divine change of mind?", "turns_on": "Whether changed law reflects changed divine knowledge or changed human circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q27/p1", "position": "No; God knew each ruling's duration and changes people's duties wisely.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī cite Abraham, Moses, Noah, Adam, and changing interests; al-Nasafī says repeal clarifies the endpoint to humans. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Biqāʿī appeal to time-dependent benefit. Biqāʿī distinguishes divine repeal from scholars' unauthorized changes to scripture."}, {"id": "2:106/q27/p2", "position": "Yes or it is impossible for divine law to be abrogated.", "reasons": "Jewish objectors equate naskh with badāʾ or late knowledge; some later Muslim groups deny possibility. Abū Muslim allows possibility while disputing Qurʾanic occurrence."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q28", "question": "Does the verse imply that the Qurʾan is created?", "turns_on": "Whether changes in words and relations reach eternal divine speech itself.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q28/p1", "position": "Yes; abrogation and differing merit imply originated speech.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazila reason that succession, removal, and divine power over replacement cannot characterize an eternal thing; al-Ṭabrisī agrees with createdness."}, {"id": "2:106/q28/p2", "position": "No; change concerns expressions or relations, not eternal inner speech.", "reasons": "Rāzī's side distinguishes words from meaning; al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes relations from essence. Al-Ālūsī challenges Rāzī's formulation because abrogation targets rulings."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q29", "question": "Why is this verse placed after the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether it answers envy of revelation, objections to changed commands, or the ban on rāʿinā.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q29/p1", "position": "It answers criticism of revelation and changed commands.", "reasons": "Polytheists or Jews accused Muhammad of contradictory commands; reports connect this verse with 16:101. Some tie the accusation to the qibla change. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Muslim instruction is primary while the Jewish objection is implicitly refuted."}, {"id": "2:106/q29/p2", "position": "It follows 2:105's denial that unbelievers wish believers any good.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā and al-Ṭabrisī take the verse as reassurance that God continues to send what is best; al-Ālūsī adds an answer to the claim that refraining from repeal would be more generous. Abū Ḥayyān notes the switch from third-person mention of God to first-person plural."}, {"id": "2:106/q29/p3", "position": "It exemplifies the immediately preceding ban on rāʿinā.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī takes that newly forbidden expression as a recent legal change; al-Ālūsī transmits the link."}, {"id": "2:106/q29/p4", "position": "It frames later changes in the sūra's detailed rulings.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥarālī sees a programmatic introduction, and al-Kashshāf links 2:107's dominion and the warning against Israelite demands to trust in God's prescription."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q30", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from changing states?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q30/p1", "position": "Successive changes raise a person to intimacy and direct address.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī invokes 53:8–10."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q31", "question": "What additional textual and methodological context do the notes give?", "turns_on": "How the surrounding source material classifies suras or transmits recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q31/p1", "position": "Sura groupings and recitation chains contextualize Qurʾanic study.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and al-Suyūṭī classify the miʾūn, mathānī and mufassal with competing starting points; al-Baghawī records reader chains and accepts their agreed readings. Ibn al-Jinnī discusses unrelated phonetic examples; al-Nashr details recitation connection and another reading."}, {"id": "2:106/q31/p2", "position": "An illustrative interpretation need not limit a verse's meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī distinguishes an example from restriction and records varying counts and classifications of abrogation."}, {"id": "2:106/q31/p3", "position": "Only the Prophet's judgment is wholly authoritative.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr uses ʿUmar's dispute with Ubayy to note that respected reciters can err; Mālik's maxim accepts or rejects everyone's view except the Prophet's."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q01", "question": "What does 'raise' mean here?", "turns_on": "The root's range includes dispatch, stirring, and revival.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q01/p1", "position": "Send or commission a messenger.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Abu Hayyan gloss baʿth as dispatch; Ibn al-Jawzi cites this verse and 62:2 for the usage."}, {"id": "2:129/q01/p2", "position": "The root can also mean rousing or reviving.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives stirring a resting she-camel and reviving; Jishumi mentions raising the dead. Ibn al-Jawzi notes Buʿath as the Aws–Khazraj battle day."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q02", "question": "Who are 'among them'?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun reaches back to Abraham's descendants or the submitted nation, to Mecca's people in 2:126, or to a narrower lineage.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q02/p1", "position": "Abraham and Ishmael's descendants, the submitted community of their line.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Thalabi, Baghawi, Tabarsi, Biqai and Bursevi specify the joint descendants; Wahidi says the two antecedents converge on Abraham's Arab descendants. Razi connects 2:128; Tabataba'i limits the requested nation to their descendants, not all believers or addressees. Asad observes that fīhim literally means 'within them'."}, {"id": "2:129/q02/p2", "position": "The people of Mecca, linked to the preceding prayer for its inhabitants.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Baghawi report the view; Ibn al-Jawzi connects it with 2:126; Abu Hayyan cites 62:2 and the unlettered. Abu Ali in Jishumi says only Muhammad among Mecca's descendants fits, unlike Israelite prophets. Alusi calls the Mecca antecedent remote."}, {"id": "2:129/q02/p3", "position": "Muhammad's community, especially Banu Hashim in al-Sadiq's report.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya and others say Muhammad's community; al-Sadiq's report identifies the community with Banu Hashim and grounds the Imams in Abraham's lineage, citing 2:127–128 and 14:35–36."}]}

{"id": "2:129/q04", "question": "Who is the requested messenger?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q04/p1", "position": "Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ and many later commentators identify him; Razi and Kuranyolu cite commentator agreement. Study Quran points to matching language in 2:151."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q05", "question": "When was Abraham's prayer fulfilled?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q05/p1", "position": "God answered it by sending Muhammad at the end of time.", "reasons": "Al-Rabiʿ and Abu al-Aliya say Abraham was told of the delayed fulfillment; Abu Hayyan says it was answered in full with Qur'anic revelation; Ibn Ashur sees fulfillment among Arabs embracing Islam before and after the Hijra despite exceptions. Muqatil cites 62:2; Study Quran cites 2:151."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q06", "question": "What did Muhammad say about this prayer and the first signs of his mission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q06/p1", "position": "He identified himself as Abraham's prayer and Jesus's glad tidings, often adding his mother's vision.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Thalabi, Baghawi, Wahidi, Razi and later works transmit forms of the statement; longer versions say his status as final prophet was written while Adam was still clay and the mother saw light reaching Syrian palaces. Wahidi, Razi, Ibn Kathir and Kuranyolu relate Jesus's announcement of Ahmad in 61:6; Abu Hayyan calls his version sound, whereas Nasafi and Alusi state no grading. Al-Dahhak locates Abraham's utterance while raising the House. Alusi says 'prayer' can mean its outcome, recipient, or emphatically the prayer itself, and Ishmael shared it despite Abraham alone being named."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q07", "question": "What does the mother's vision of Syrian light signify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q07/p1", "position": "It foretells the mission's reach and faith's later refuge in Syria.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says the vision was a pregnancy dream that spread among her people; Syria would be a refuge near the end, Jesus would descend by Damascus's eastern white minaret, and a report says a group would remain on truth there. Other accounts simply report light illuminating Syria's palaces; Ibn Kathir adds that prophets' mothers have such visions."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q08", "question": "What lineage and wider scriptural announcements are connected with this messenger?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ on the specified people and on how the later lineage and announcements are described.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q08/p1", "position": "Muhammad is traced through Ishmael's Arabized descendants, and earlier scripture is said to announce him.", "reasons": "Baghawi and Abu Hayyan transmit Ibn Abbas's ten non-Israelite prophets, though Abu Hayyan notes his excerpt lists nine. Kuranyolu recounts Ishmael's settlement among Jurhum, twelve children, the Mustaʿriba, and Adnan as Muhammad's twenty-first ancestor; it reports Muslim readings of John's Paraclete and earlier scriptural announcements, citing 7:157 and 61:6."}, {"id": "2:129/q08/p2", "position": "Bursevi calls this an invocation for a messenger among the Israelites.", "reasons": "This is Bursevi's specific formulation, despite his nearby identification of Muhammad as the answer."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q09", "question": "What does rasūl mean and how is it derived?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate etymon is the message or the camel's forward movement.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q09/p1", "position": "A sent messenger, on faʿūl from risāla.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Qurtubi derive it from message or dispatch; dispatched parties are rusul, arrivals in succession irsālan, and milk rasl because it flows from the udder."}, {"id": "2:129/q09/p2", "position": "It may derive from a camel moving easily ahead of others.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari supplies marsāl or rasla; Thalabi and Qurtubi add dispatched groups and successive arrivals as related usage."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q10", "question": "What does Ubayy's reading add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q10/p1", "position": "It adds 'among their later generations'.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit Ubayy's wording; Alusi takes it as supporting Muhammad's identification."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q11", "question": "How are ibʿath, fīhim and minhum parsed?", "turns_on": "Which expression the prepositional phrase attaches to.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q11/p1", "position": "Ibʿath is coordinated with tab; fīhim modifies ibʿath or an implied 'messenger among them'.", "reasons": "Tabarsi gives both attachments and treats the latter as circumstantial. Asad notes the literal 'within them'."}, {"id": "2:129/q11/p2", "position": "Minhum is an accusative adjective of rasūlan with an implicit attachment.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin infer 'a messenger belonging to them'; it stresses the messenger's origin among his audience."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q12", "question": "How is yatlū parsed?", "turns_on": "The clause may describe the messenger, state his circumstance, or hypothetically answer the imperative.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q12/p1", "position": "It is an accusative adjective of rasūlan.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Tabarsi give this parse; al-Samin prefers it as the best order. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi also allow it."}, {"id": "2:129/q12/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial of rasūlan or its already specified referent.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi allow the circumstantial parse. Al-Samin says the prior minhum adjective makes rasūlan specific enough."}, {"id": "2:129/q12/p3", "position": "It is circumstantial of the pronoun in minhum.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says the implied existential verb governs the circumstantial clause."}, {"id": "2:129/q12/p4", "position": "Outside recitation it could be jussive as the prayer's response.", "reasons": "Nahhas marks this as a non-Qur'anic grammatical possibility."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q13", "question": "How are the verbs after yatlū connected?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q13/p1", "position": "They are coordinated with yatlū.", "reasons": "Nahhas parses teaching the Book and wisdom and purifying them as coordinated verbs."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q14", "question": "How is 'wa-yuʿallimuhum' pronounced or read?", "turns_on": "The phonetic status of the weakened vowel and the Hijazi–Tamimi usage.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q14/p1", "position": "The mīm's vowel can be faintly shortened, rather than wholly absent.", "reasons": "Abu ʿAmr lightly rounds or lowers the vowel before hāʾ; al-Farisi says omitted vowel remains grammatically intended and only ḍamma/kasra permit ikhtilās. Sībawayh treats the apparent sukūn as faint pronunciation. Ibn Jinni attributes light forms to Tamim and explains vowel loss by clustered movements; Abū Zayd's yaktubūn and Abū ʿAmr's bāriʾikum are parallels. Ibn Jinni also defends an actually still mīm from Sībawayh's hearing and poetic meter against Abu al-ʿAbbas."}, {"id": "2:129/q14/p2", "position": "Hijazi usage geminates the relevant forms.", "reasons": "Abu ʿAmr as transmitted by Ibn Jinni contrasts Hijazi gemination of yuʿallimuhum and yalʿanuhum with light Tamimi forms; Ibn Jinni says gemination needs no special defense."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q15", "question": "How is the implied speech construction explained?", "turns_on": "Whether qawl is syntactically ellipted or supplied by the sense of an overt verb.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q15/p1", "position": "An implicit qawl is omitted.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni sides with the Basrans; Ibn Masʿud's cited reading makes the speech verb overt. His parallels include a poem, calling Antarah, and the angels' greeting; the poem's meter and Sībawayh's transmission answer Abu al-ʿAbbas's objection."}, {"id": "2:129/q15/p2", "position": "The existing wording itself carries the sense of speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni reports the Kufan account: akhbarānā can itself mean qālā lanā, without an omitted verb."}]}

{"id": "2:129/q18", "question": "Why mention recitation before teaching, and how do the tasks differ?", "turns_on": "Whether the clauses describe stages, functions, or several aspects of one scripture.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q18/p1", "position": "Recitation gives the wording and proof; teaching supplies meaning and practice.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi say recitation establishes the Qur'an's inimitability and prophecy, while teaching explains law, unity, justice and evidence. Razi says recitation preserves wording by mass transmission, guards against alteration and is worship in prayer; teaching its proofs, rulings and secrets is the higher goal. Abu Hayyan says hearing precedes reflection, and details teaching of lawful/forbidden, duties, parables, promises, threats and the afterlife. Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya say the Prophet supplies material and methods for inquiry."}, {"id": "2:129/q18/p2", "position": "The Book's descriptions as recited signs, written scripture and proof can overlap.", "reasons": "Thalabi cites al-Hutayʾa for coordinating distinct descriptions; Jishumi reports 'written' and 'proof' as descriptions of one Book. Qurtubi distinguishes its wording, meanings and intended rulings as signs, Book and wisdom."}, {"id": "2:129/q18/p3", "position": "Teaching may cause understanding or may only provide its means.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan explains why a learner does not necessarily learn; the Messenger communicates and facilitates, while God grants understanding."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q19", "question": "What is 'the Book' here?", "turns_on": "Whether kitāb denotes the revealed Qur'an, writing as a skill, or a part of scripture.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q19/p1", "position": "The Qur'an.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd, Hasan and many others identify it; Ibn Abbas in Wahidi includes its duties, rulings, Sunnah and earlier prophetic laws. Biqai calls it comprehensive of scriptures and recalls comprehensive speech; Alusi says the requested scripture need not have been explicitly named Qur'an before its answer."}, {"id": "2:129/q19/p2", "position": "Writing with the pen.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports this alternative from Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "2:129/q19/p3", "position": "The unambiguous verses, while wisdom designates ambiguous verses.", "reasons": "Razi reports this division within scripture."}]}
{"id": "2:129/q20", "question": "What is the wisdom taught by the messenger?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired term is prophetic instruction outside the Book, Qur'anic content, learned and lived discernment, judgment, or a distinct spiritual quality.", "positions": [{"id": "2:129/q20/p1", "position": "The Prophet's Sunnah and explanation of law.", "reasons": "Qatada, al-Shafi'i and many commentators identify it; Shafi'i's followers argue separation from the Book marks extra-scriptural teaching and reply that rational proofs are independently accessible. Abu Hayyan says Sunnah clarifies generalities, ambiguities and omitted details and supplies further rulings; a report says the Prophet was given Qur'an and twice as much wisdom. Ibn Kathir treats religious understanding as compatible. Alusi challenges the assertion that soul-perfecting truths must lie outside the Qur'an, citing 6:38 and 16:89."}, {"id": "2:129/q20/p2", "position": "Religious knowledge, understanding and observance, especially rulings known through the Messenger.", "reasons": "Malik and Ibn Zayd describe knowledge, fiqh and following it; Ibn Zayd calls it divinely placed heart-light and cites 2:269, 3:48 and 7:175 to show signs without wisdom do not benefit. Tabari prefers prophetic clarification of God's rulings. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add innate insight; Biqai describes all prescribed commands as wisdom protecting worldly and afterlife paths. Razi says this includes benefit and interpretation."}, {"id": "2:129/q20/p3", "position": "The Qur'an itself, its understanding, admonitions and lawful and forbidden matters.", "reasons": "Muqatil stresses exhortation and halal/haram; Mujahid stresses understanding; Wahidi and others treat wisdom as another name or quality of the Book, sometimes repeated for emphasis. Razi reports its embedded rationale and benefit; Alusi distinguishes its wording from inner truths. Thalabi's al-Hutayʾa line supports coordination of synonymous content."}, {"id": "2:129/q20/p4", "position": "Sound knowledge joined to right action, speech and conduct.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and Abd Allah ibn Muslim require both; Abu Jaʿfar says sound speech yields sound action or state; Razi adds putting each thing in its place; Baydawi and Elmalili connect it with perfection of the soul and 2:269."}, {"id": "2:129/q20/p5", "position": "An admonishing saying that restrains evil and urges virtue.", "reasons": "Al-Buraydi, Ibn Durayd and others include rebuke and guidance; the Prophetic saying 'some poetry is wisdom' supports it.
